title: Observable-targeted variational quantum simulation of Hamiltonian dynamics
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Luciano Pereira, Antonio Acín
abstract: Standard variational quantum simulation seeks to reproduce the evolution of the full quantum state, although many applications require only the expectation values of a few observables. We study a variational method for pure-state Hamiltonian dynamics that updates circuit parameters to reproduce the evolution of selected expectation values. An exact error identity guides the choice of observables, motivating a construction based on repeated commutators of the target with the Hamiltonian. For Pauli observables and Pauli-rotation circuits, the update can be estimated without ancillary qubits or controlled operations for overlap estimation. Across six-qubit spin, fermionic, and molecular benchmarks, the targeted update extends the median time within the target-error tolerance by up to a factor of $4.2$ relative to standard variational quantum simulation at equal shot budgets. These results show that directing the variational update toward the target observable can extend accurate simulation without increasing the measurement cost per time step.
summary: This paper introduces an observable-targeted variational quantum simulation technique that focuses parameter updates on matching the evolution of specific target observables rather than the entire quantum state. By leveraging an error identity, the method significantly extends the simulation time achievable with limited measurement resources compared to standard approaches. This advancement is particularly valuable for simulating complex strongly correlated electron systems like the Hubbard model.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics when only the expectation values of a few observables are needed, rather than the full quantum state.
main_result: The proposed observable-targeted variational quantum simulation method extends the median time within the target-error tolerance by up to a factor of 4.2 compared to standard VQS at equal measurement budgets.
method: It updates variational circuit parameters by minimizing the mismatch in the equations of motion for a selected set of target observables, guided by an exact error identity.
model_or_system: The method is benchmarked across several models, including six-qubit spin systems (Ising, XXZ, XY), the Fermi-Hubbard model, and molecular Hamiltonians (LiH).
key_observables: The target observable A, and the set of observables O used to construct the update dictionary (often involving repeated commutators with the Hamiltonian).
important_parameters: Measurement budgets (shot counts $S$), target error tolerance ($\epsilon$), and the number of parameters ($p$) and dictionary size ($K$).
main_assumptions: The method relies on the assumption that the error can be effectively projected onto the subspace spanned by the target observables, and it uses finite measurement statistics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the cycle of the targeted VQS: observables guide selection, the quantum processor measures data, and the classical processor determines parameter velocities to match the target observable dynamics.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by contrasting standard VQS (state-level objective) with the proposed observable-targeted approach (seminorm minimization). It details the mathematical formulation using the target error identity and applies the method to various physical models.
why_interesting: This work directly improves the resource scaling of quantum simulation algorithms by making the variational optimization process physically informed, which is crucial for simulating complex, strongly correlated materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Observable-targeted variational quantum simulation. The Hamiltonian and target observables guide the selection of observables to track. The quantum processor prepares variational states and collects measurement data. The classical processor determines angle velocities that approximately reproduce the selected observable dynamics, advances the circuit angles, and returns them to the quantum processor. This cycle repeats until the final time, when the target expectation values are measured.
